topic: Geometry (Lines, Angles, Triangles, Circles & Coordinate Geometry)

items.title: Lines, Angles & Parallel-Line Pairs
items.body:
When two **parallel lines** are cut by a transversal, eight angles form in predictable pairs. Picture two horizontal parallel lines with a slanting transversal crossing both: at each crossing there are four angles, and the two crossings mirror each other.

| Angle pair | Position | Relation |
|---|---|---|
| Corresponding | same corner at each crossing | equal |
| Alternate interior | opposite sides, between the lines | equal |
| Alternate exterior | opposite sides, outside the lines | equal |
| Co-interior (allied) | same side, between the lines | supplementary (180°) |

**Basic angle facts:** complementary sum to 90°, supplementary to 180°; a linear pair on a straight line sums to 180°; vertically opposite angles are equal; angles round a point sum to 360°.

**Worked example:** allied angles (2x+20) and (3x−30) between parallel lines → sum 180° → 5x−10=180 → x=38 → angles 96° and 84°.

**Trap:** co-interior angles are supplementary, NOT equal — only corresponding/alternate pairs are equal.
keyPoints: Corresponding and alternate angles between parallel lines are equal.
Co-interior (same-side interior) angles are supplementary, summing to 180°.
Complementary angles sum to 90°; supplementary and linear-pair angles sum to 180°.
Vertically opposite angles are equal; angles around a point total 360°.
items.source: Quantitative Reasoning — Concept of Point and Line; Angles

items.title: Triangles — Angles, Pythagoras, Similarity
items.body:
**Angle rules:** interior angles sum to 180°; an exterior angle equals the sum of the two remote interior angles; the largest angle faces the longest side.

**Triangle inequality:** each side lies strictly between the difference and sum of the other two. With sides 5 and 9, the third side satisfies 4 < s < 14.

**Pythagoras (right triangles only):** hyp² = base² + height². Memorise triples: 3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17, 7-24-25 (and their multiples, e.g. 9-12-15).

**Similarity vs congruence:** similar = same shape, sides proportional (tests AA, SSS-proportional, SAS-proportional); congruent = identical (SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS, RHS).

| Ratio quantity | Scaling with side ratio k |
|---|---|
| Corresponding sides / perimeter | k |
| Area | k² |
| Volume (solids) | k³ |

**Worked example:** similar triangles with sides 3:5, smaller area 36 → larger area = 36×(5/3)² = 36×25/9 = 100.

**Trap:** when sides scale by k, area scales by k² (not k) — do not apply the side ratio directly to areas.
keyPoints: Triangle interior angles sum to 180°; exterior angle = sum of two remote interior angles.
Triangle inequality: third side lies strictly between the difference and sum of the other two.
Pythagoras applies only to right triangles: hyp² = base² + height².
For similar triangles, areas scale as the square of the side ratio (k²).
items.source: Quantitative Reasoning — Basic concept of Triangle; Similarity & Congruency

items.title: Triangle Centres & the Angle Bisector Theorem
items.body:
A triangle has four classic concurrency points:

| Centre | Formed by | Key property |
|---|---|---|
| Centroid (G) | the 3 medians | divides each median 2:1 from the vertex; centre of mass |
| Incentre (I) | the 3 angle bisectors | equidistant from the sides; centre of inscribed circle |
| Circumcentre (O) | perpendicular bisectors of sides | equidistant from vertices; centre of circumscribed circle |
| Orthocentre (H) | the 3 altitudes | intersection of altitudes |

**Right-triangle specials:** circumcentre = midpoint of the hypotenuse; orthocentre = the right-angle vertex. Inradius of a right triangle r = (a + b − c)/2 (legs a, b; hypotenuse c), equivalently r = Area/s.

**Angle bisector theorem:** the bisector from A meets BC at D with BD : DC = AB : AC.

**Worked example:** AB=6, AC=8, BC=14 → BD:DC = 6:8 = 3:4 → BD = 14×3/7 = 6, DC = 8.

**Trap:** the centroid split is 2:1 measured *from the vertex*, so vertex-to-G is the larger (2/3) part.
keyPoints: Centroid divides each median in ratio 2:1 from the vertex.
Circumcentre of a right triangle is the midpoint of the hypotenuse; orthocentre is the right-angle vertex.
Incentre is the meeting of angle bisectors and is always inside the triangle.
Angle bisector theorem: BD:DC = AB:AC for the bisector from A to BC.
items.source: Quantitative Reasoning — Centroid; Circumcentre; Angle Bisector

items.title: Circles & Polygon Angles
items.body:
**Circle angle theorems:** the central angle is twice any inscribed angle on the same arc; the angle in a semicircle is 90°; angles in the same segment are equal; opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral sum to 180°.

**Tangent & chord:** a tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact, so tangent length from an external point at distance d = √(d² − r²); the two tangents from an external point are equal. Alternate-segment: the angle between a tangent and a chord equals the inscribed angle in the alternate segment.

**Worked example (tangent):** d=13, r=5 → tangent = √(169−25) = √144 = 12.

**Polygon angles:** for n sides — sum of interior angles = (n−2)×180°; sum of exterior angles = 360° (always). Regular polygon: each interior = (n−2)×180°/n, each exterior = 360°/n.

**Worked example (polygon):** each exterior 24° → n = 360/24 = 15 sides; interior sum = 13×180 = 2340°.

**Trap:** exterior angles always total 360° regardless of n — use that to find sides quickly.
keyPoints: Central angle = 2 × inscribed angle on the same arc; angle in a semicircle = 90°.
Tangent ⊥ radius at contact; tangent length = √(d² − r²); two tangents from a point are equal.
Sum of interior angles of an n-gon = (n−2)×180°.
Sum of exterior angles of any polygon = 360°; regular polygon exterior = 360°/n.
items.source: Quantitative Reasoning — Basic concept of Circle; Theorems of circle; Angles

items.title: Coordinate Geometry — Distance, Section, Slope & Area
items.body:
Core formulas for points in the plane:

| Quantity | Formula |
|---|---|
| Distance A(x₁,y₁)–B(x₂,y₂) | √[(x₂−x₁)² + (y₂−y₁)²] |
| Midpoint | ((x₁+x₂)/2, (y₁+y₂)/2) |
| Section (ratio m:n internally) | ((mx₂+nx₁)/(m+n), (my₂+ny₁)/(m+n)) |
| Slope | m = (y₂−y₁)/(x₂−x₁) |
| Area of triangle | ½·\|x₁(y₂−y₃)+x₂(y₃−y₁)+x₃(y₁−y₂)\| |

**Line relations:** parallel lines have equal slopes; perpendicular lines have m₁·m₂ = −1; three points are collinear iff the triangle area = 0.

**Worked examples:** distance (2,3)–(7,15) = √(25+144)=13; point dividing (2,3)–(7,−2) in 2:3 = (4,1); slope of (1,2)–(4,11) = 9/3 = 3; area of (0,0),(4,0),(0,6) = ½×4×6 = 12.

**Trap:** in the section formula the ratio weights cross over — m multiplies the *second* point's coordinates, n the first.
keyPoints: Distance = √[(Δx)² + (Δy)²]; midpoint = average of the coordinates.
Section formula (m:n internally): ((mx₂+nx₁)/(m+n), (my₂+ny₁)/(m+n)).
Slope m = Δy/Δx; parallel lines equal slopes, perpendicular lines m₁·m₂ = −1.
Triangle area = ½|x₁(y₂−y₃)+x₂(y₃−y₁)+x₃(y₁−y₂)|; zero area means collinear.

items.title: Tangent pairs, tangential quadrilaterals & integer-triangle counting
items.body:
## Two tangents from an external point

- The two tangents from a point P are **equal in length**, and each is ⟂ to the radius at its contact point.
- In quadrilateral P–A–O–B (A, B contact points, O centre): **∠APB + ∠AOB = 180°** (two right angles at A and B use up the rest).

**Worked example.** Angle between tangents ∠P = 70° ⇒ central angle ∠AOB = 180° − 70° = **110°**.

## Tangential quadrilateral (incircle touching all sides)

- **AB + CD = BC + AD** — the two sums of opposite sides are equal (equal tangent lengths from each vertex).

**Worked example.** AB = 8, BC = 9, CD = 7 ⇒ AD = (8 + 7) − 9 = **6**.

## Counting integer-sided triangles for a fixed perimeter

- List unordered triples **a ≤ b ≤ c** with a + b + c = P and the triangle inequality **a + b > c**.
- Shortcut: the largest side satisfies **c < P/2**.

**Worked example (P = 14).** c ≤ 6 → (2,6,6),(3,5,6),(4,4,6),(4,5,5) = **4 triangles** (not 5 — (2,5,7) fails 2+5>7).
keyPoints: Two tangents from a point are equal; ∠between tangents + central angle = 180°.
Tangential quadrilateral: AB + CD = BC + AD (opposite-side sums equal).
Integer-triangle count: list a ≤ b ≤ c, sum = P, with a + b > c.
Largest side c < P/2; perimeter 14 gives exactly 4 integer triangles.
items.mnemonic: Tangents: ∠P + ∠O = 180°. Tangential quad: opposite sides sum equal. Counting: c < P/2 and a+b>c.
items.source: Quantitative Reasoning — Theorems of circle; Triangle inequality
